cards.headline:
AI emulators could speed up
weather and climate models
cards.body: LLNL trains neural-network emulators like STRATA on E3SM output to predict the atmosphere without solving equations.

blocks.cap: The STRATA emulator aims to accurately predict long-term weather without computationally expensive and time-intensive simulations. Credit: Graphic by Peter Caldwell

blocks.x: Modeling a decade into the future takes months on the world's best supercomputers. At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), researchers are deploying emulators to provide faster and more accurate weather predictions, months to years into the future.

E3SM can simulate the atmosphere at 3-kilometer resolution by solving physics equations. Instead, scientists from LLNL, DOE and NVIDIA train an emulator named STRATA on the outputs from a model like E3SM, then ask it to predict how the atmosphere looks days to months to years later—without ever solving the physics equations. "For an emulator, we use machine learning, like a deep neural network, to mimic what the real physics would have done," said LLNL scientist Yunyan Zhang.

blocks.cap: The STRATA emulator 12-hour forecast (top row) compared to the Simple Cloud-Resolving E3SM Atmosphere Model (SCREAM, bottom row). Credit: Graphic by Peter Caldwell

blocks.x: The speed lets scientists run hundreds of simulations to weigh many predictions at once. For the Los Alamos-led MAGGIE project, which uses generative models to create initial conditions, "it would have taken us three months to do this ensemble of simulations with a physics-based model," said Peter Caldwell. "With our new emulators, we did it over a weekend."

Through the DOE Genesis Mission, the STITCH project, led by Zhang, trains emulators on localized simulations of cloud microphysics and small-scale turbulence; their results can be fed into E3SM, which in turn provides new training data for STRATA.
